persona.who: 39, Indian-American, two kids, runs a dental practice with her husband, loses her temper with the kids and hates herself after.
persona.note: I yelled at my 7 year old this morning for spilling milk and the look on his face. I am turning into my mother. I run a practice, I manage 12 people calmly, and then at home I just snap

understanding.emotion: ashamed and terrified of becoming her mother
understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call anger that takes over, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: From the look on your son's face to the breath before you speak, the week turns the verdict you pass on yourself into a practice you can actually use.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the snap and the shame, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the anger and the regret are the same thing in two movements, and the fear is the verdict you pass on yourself.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the steadiness is not the absence of anger but the space between the snap and the next breath.
week_beats.act: You try stopping before you speak to your son, breathing once, and naming what is blocked wanting underneath the anger.
week_beats.story: A mother who snapped at her child and then chose a different way shows you what changing what you pass on looks like.

understanding.core_struggle: A working mother who manages twelve people calmly at work snaps at her seven-year-old at home, and the shame of it is the fear she is becoming her own mother.
understanding.mirror: What you told us: yelled at her seven-year-old for spilling milk.
understanding.insight: The anger arrives before you choose it. By the time you notice, it has already spoken for you.

queries.hook: The shame of snapping at your child and the terror that you are becoming the mother you did not want to be, even when you manage everyone else well.
queries.diagnose: Anger rises from blocked wanting; it clouds judgement, and a clouded mind says and does what it later regrets.
queries.steady: Praise and blame, success and failure, come and go like the seasons; what is yours to hold is the steadiness between them, not the storm.
queries.act: Before you speak to your son again, stop; breathe; and ask what is blocked wanting underneath the anger, then name it to yourself.
queries.story: A mother who managed her household well and then snapped at her child, faced the look on his face, and found the courage to change what she passed on.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse.sanskrit: सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति । वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते ॥ गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते । न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः ॥
verse.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.
verse.why: Even the strongest people freeze; the Gita begins with a breakdown, not a hero.
verse.misuse: Not a dismissal of anxiety; it shows that even the strong feel it, and the teaching starts there.

prasang.title: Overcome by delusion, Arjuna speaks in fear, love and grief
prasang.summary: Seeing his kin ready to die, Arjuna trembles, his bow slips, and he argues that no victory is worth killing family. He sits down in the chariot and refuses to fight.
prasang.story_hook: The greatest archer of his age stood between two armies, and his hands began to shake.
prasang.lesson: Even the strongest people freeze; the Gita begins with a breakdown, not a hero.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands in his chariot between two armies. He looks at the faces before him and sees his own kin. His hands shake. His mouth goes dry. His body trembles and his hair stands on end. He is not a hero at this moment. He is a man who has lost his footing. The Gita opens with a breakdown, not a battle cry. It says that even the strongest people freeze. The teaching does not begin with strength. It begins with the truth that you can collapse and still be heard.
verse.for_you: You manage twelve people calmly all day and then snap at your seven-year-old. The shame of it is real. This verse says that even the strongest people freeze. Your breakdown is not a failure. It is the place where the teaching begins.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
verse.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Krishna is answering Arjuna's question about what a steady person looks like. He explains that when you fix your thoughts on something, you start to feel attached. That attachment grows into a deep wanting. When that wanting is blocked, it turns into anger. The verse says anger does not come from nowhere. It starts with where your mind has been dwelling.
verse.for_you: The anger that arrives at your child's face and the shame that follows are two movements of the same moment. The fear that you are becoming her is the verdict you pass on yourself after the fact. See the pattern: the anger takes over, and then your mind judges you for it.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse.sanskrit: जितात्मनः प्रशान्तस्य परमात्मा समाहितः । शीतोष्णसुखदुःखेषु तथा मानापमानयोः ॥
verse.line: Self-mastered and calm, you stay centred in heat and cold, pleasure and pain, praise and insult.
verse.translation: For one who has conquered himself and is at peace, the higher self stays steady in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour.
verse.why: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.
verse.misuse: Staying steady under insult is not accepting mistreatment; you can stay calm and still speak up.

prasang.title: Lift yourself by yourself; marks of the realised
prasang.summary: Raise yourself by yourself; you are your own friend or enemy. The self-mastered person stays calm in heat and cold, praise and blame, and sees friend and foe alike.
prasang.lesson: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.

verse.for_you: The steadiness is not the absence of anger. It is the space between the snap and the next breath. You can hold that space. You can be your own best friend in that moment, not your worst enemy.

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Just told he is exiled, Ram calms his furious brother Lakshman.
verse.sanskrit: निगृह्य रोष शोकं च धैर्यमाश्रित्य केवलम्। अवमानं निरस्यैनं गृहीत्वा हर्षमुत्तमम्॥ उपक्लुप्तं यदैतन्मे अभिषेकार्थमुत्तमम्। सर्वं निवर्तय क्षिप्रं कुरु कार्य निरव्ययम्॥
verse.line: Rein in anger and grief, lean on your steadiness, and set the insult aside.
verse.translation: Hold back your anger and grief, lean on steadiness alone, set this insult aside and take up real cheerfulness. Quickly undo the preparations made for my coronation and get on with what needs doing, without fuss.
verse.why: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.
verse.misuse: Not a call to ignore injustice; it is about choosing your response.

prasang.title: Lakshman's fury, Ram's calm
prasang.summary: Lakshman is enraged by the injustice and wants to seize the throne by force. Ram calms him: set aside the insult, don't torment yourself, the setback may lead somewhere better. Lakshman answers that effort, not fate, decides; both views are given their due.
prasang.lesson: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.

verse.meaning: Ram has just been told he must leave the kingdom and go to the forest for fourteen years. His brother Lakshman is burning with rage, ready to fight the whole court and take the throne by force. Ram tells him to rein in his anger and grief, to lean on steadiness alone, and to set this insult aside. He asks Lakshman to undo the coronation preparations and move forward without fuss. The verse says that anger at injustice is natural, but you could decide what to do with it before it decides for you.
verse.for_you: Anger is a passing fire in the mind; you can watch it rise and fall without letting it speak for you.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Yudhishthira
verse.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
verse.sanskrit: आत्मानं च परांश्चैव त्रायते महतो भयात् / क्रुध्यन्तमप्रतिक्रुध्यन्दूयोरेष चिकित्सकः
verse.line: Don't answer anger with anger. The one who stays calm protects both people, and heals both.
verse.translation: One who does not get angry back at an angry person saves both himself and the other from great danger. He becomes the healer of both.
verse.why: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
verse.misuse: Staying calm is not the same as staying in a situation where you are unsafe.

prasang.title: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.story_hook: Thirteen years into exile, Draupadi looked at her husband and asked why he was not angry.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

verse.meaning: In the forest, Draupadi is furious at the injustice done to her family and tells Yudhishthira to answer force with force. He replies that one who does not get angry back at an angry person saves both himself and the other from great danger. He becomes the healer of both. The verse says that anger rarely heals anything. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
verse.for_you: Pause before you speak, hold back the harsh word, and answer anger with calm; forgive so the fire does not keep burning in you.

verse.speaker: Bhishma
verse.setting: Gautama orders his son Chirakari, 'the slow one', to kill his mother; the son deliberates, and saves them all.
verse.sanskrit: एवं सर्वेषु कार्येषु विमृश्य पुरुषस्ततः / चिरेण निश्चयं कृत्वा चिरं न परितप्यते
verse.line: Think it over and decide slowly, and you'll spend far less time in regret.
verse.translation: So, in every matter, a person should think it over and decide slowly; then he does not suffer regret for long.
verse.why: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

prasang.title: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.story_hook: Ordered by his furious father to kill his mother, Chirakari did what he always did: he thought about it.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

verse.meaning: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira this while they are in the forest. He speaks of a sage named Gautama who orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother in a jealous rage, then storms off. Chirakari, known for his slowness, thinks so carefully about a father's command and a mother's life that he delays the act. Gautama returns in regret, and they are all saved. Bhishma says that when anger rises, or when someone you love seems to have wronged you, you could think it over and decide slowly.
verse.for_you: You are the witness of the anger, not the anger; the fire rises in the mind, but the one who sees it is untouched.

script: You manage twelve people calmly all day and then snap at your seven-year-old. The shame of it is real.

Arjuna stands in his chariot between two armies. He looks at the faces before him and sees his own kin. His hands shake. His mouth goes dry. His body trembles and his hair stands on end. He is not a hero at this moment. He is a man who has lost his footing. And Arjuna said:
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति, वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते. गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते, न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः.
In plain words: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.

This is what happens when anger takes over. By the time you notice, it has already spoken for you. Your body knows before your mind does. This is easier said than done, because the anger arrives before you choose it. You are left holding the regret.
Tonight, before you go to your child, take one breath. Feel your feet on the floor. Let the anger sit there without moving. You do not have to fix it right now.
You can collapse and still be heard.

depth.life: You carry the weight of twelve people all day, and by evening the wire is frayed. The shame of snapping at your seven-year-old sits in your chest like a stone. You fear the face of your mother looking back at you from your own tired eyes.
depth.points: What you feel is not weakness. It is a body that has reached its limit. The texts say even the strongest person can freeze. The anger that takes over is not who you are. It is a storm that passes through you, and it does not define your heart.
depth.practice: Before you speak to your child tonight, pause and feel your feet on the floor. Name one thing you can see in the room.
depth.question: What if the anger is not you, but a signal your body has sent?
